name: Chloe Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a refrigerated truck for a regional dairy. Milk, yoghurt, butter and cream, out to schools, cafés and village shops on a loop of about twelve drops. I start at six, load from the cold store, and I'm done by two, which I love. The cold is what wears me out, in and out of the fridge box all morning, and the school kitchens that never have anyone at the back door.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to drive, and how settled do you feel?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a waitress, then a delivery van driver, and the dairy put me through my truck licence a year and a half ago. I'm still learning the lanes and I scraped a wing mirror on a gatepost in September. I live with my boyfriend Tom, he's a mechanic at a tyre and exhaust garage, and we've got about three months of bills saved for a house deposit we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave things as they are. I'm not someone who posts much, but I'd tell the girls at the dairy I'm glad nobody's making me learn another gadget. People need milk, that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job and keep getting better at it. The dairy still gives me a paper delivery note with the school cook's scribbles on the back, and I hope it always will. My worry is more the summer holidays, when the schools close and my hours drop a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, same route, same truck. I'd try to pick up a couple of café runs over summer to cover the school holidays. And Tom and I would keep putting 200 a month towards the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the summer drop actually hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's about six weeks of shorter days, so maybe a fifth less pay. We plan for it now, so it's annoying rather than scary. Tom does overtime in summer because everyone's tyres go before holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing that would actually worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dairy losing the schools contract. Our manager Linda says the council puts it out to tender every three years. If someone cheaper wins, my route goes.

say: I'd say **leave things** as they are; people still need milk.
I'd tell the girls at the dairy I'm glad there's **no new gadget** to learn.
think: I keep my job and keep **getting better** at it.
The **summer holidays** cut my hours when the schools close.
do: Keep the same **route** and the same truck.
Pick up **café runs** over summer to cover the school break.
Keep saving **200 a month** with Tom for a deposit.
S0.quote: The dairy still gives me a paper delivery note with the school cook's scribbles on the back, and I hope it always will.
fieldNote: Chloe values the **paper and routine** of her job and wants it untouched.
Her real risk is the **schools contract** going to a cheaper bidder.
She and her boyfriend have already **planned around** the summer dip.

steps.text: Keep the same twelve-drop dairy route
Pick up café runs during the school summer holidays
Keep saving 200 a month with Tom for a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, I suppose, but they can keep it away from me. At work I'd moan about the tablet every morning. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just grumble to Tom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learnt to drive a lorry so I could stop staring at screens, and now the dairy wants me tapping a tablet at every school kitchen door. The office will use AI for orders and routes, and the schools will order online. My driving's fine, but I'd be slower than the others on the gadgets, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tablet training because I'd have to, and I'd ask Linda to sit with me for the first week. I wouldn't do anything extra. I'd keep saving and wait to see how it settles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the dairy would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sue in the order office, definitely. She takes the calls from the cafés and knows everyone's quirks. If the computer does that, she's gone, and then who do I ring when a café owner shouts at me?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see. Is there a point where you'd act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started timing us on the tablet and I kept coming last, then yes, I'd look around. Probably at another dairy or a bakery run where things are still old-fashioned. I'm not proud, I just like what I know.

say: I'd say it's **progress**, I suppose, but keep it away from me.
I'd **grumble** to my boyfriend rather than post anything online.
think: The office moves orders and routes to AI, and I end up **tapping a tablet**.
I'd be **slower** on the gadgets than other drivers, which worries me.
do: Do the **tablet training** and ask Linda to sit with me the first week.
Keep saving and **wait to see** how things settle.
Look at **other dairies** if the tablet times me and I'm last.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a sense of being left behind.
S1.quote: I learnt to drive a lorry so I could stop staring at screens, and now the dairy wants me tapping a tablet at every school kitchen door.
fieldNote: Chloe chose driving partly to **escape screens**, so office AI feels personal.
She worries for **Sue** in orders as her link to difficult customers.
Her trigger to act is being **ranked last** by the tablet.

steps.text: Do the dairy's tablet training with Linda for the first week
Wait to see how the tablet system settles before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and the government needs to sort something out for people like us. I'd say it to Tom, my mum, the girls at work. I don't think I'd go on marches, but I'd vote for whoever had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the truck around 2031, I think, maybe sooner if they fit those self-driving fridge trucks first. My boyfriend Tom fixes exhausts, and a garage with no drivers probably needs fewer exhausts fixed, so we'd both be in trouble. The house deposit would just stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the deposit money into a separate account and not touch it, as our emergency fund. I'd ask Tom's boss whether I could start learning tyre fitting at the garage, because at least it's a place I know. And I'd vote for whoever promises proper help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest goes tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes first and the robots three years later. Does that gap help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because my bit is all hands, lifting crates. But I don't use any AI, so I wouldn't be ready for the office changes in 2028. I'd just be driving and waiting for the bad news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to worry, and she'd worry anyway. She cleaned offices for thirty years and she'd say people always find a way. I'd want to believe her.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and the government must sort something out.
I'd **vote** for whoever had a plan rather than march.
think: I'd lose the **truck** around 2031, maybe earlier if fridge trucks go first.
My boyfriend's **garage** would need fewer repairs too, so we'd both struggle.
do: Move the deposit savings into a **separate emergency** account.
Ask Tom's boss about **learning tyre fitting** at the garage.
S2.quote: My boyfriend Tom fixes exhausts, and a garage with no drivers probably needs fewer exhausts fixed, so we'd both be in trouble.
fieldNote: Chloe sees **both incomes** at risk because her boyfriend's trade depends on drivers.
The **deposit** turns into an emergency fund straight away.
She admits she'd be **unready** for the 2028 office changes because she avoids AI.

steps.text: Move the house deposit into a separate emergency account
Ask the garage owner about learning tyre fitting
Vote for candidates with a plan for drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not panic. I'd probably say the same as I said for the slow one, that people need milk. Online I wouldn't say anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough that I'd probably tell myself it's not real for the first three. Robots around 2034 gives me until I'm 35 on the truck. I know that's me being lazy, but that's honestly what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and saving, and in about year three I'd start looking seriously at the garage. Maybe I'd do a tyre-fitting course at weekends by then. Tom and I would probably still buy a small house, but a cheaper one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in the background. Like a dentist appointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start before year three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it happen to someone I know. If Sue in the office lost her job in the first year, I'd start then. I learn by watching other people get burnt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a cheaper house rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent is money gone and a house is something. If we buy a small one with a low mortgage, we could live on one wage if we had to. My dad always said never stretch.

say: I'd say there's **time**, so let's not panic.
I'd repeat that people **need milk** and keep quiet online.
think: I'd tell myself it's **not real** for the first three years.
Robots around **2034** keep me on the truck until I'm 35.
do: Keep driving and **saving** for the first few years.
Start a weekend **tyre-fitting** course around year three.
Buy a **cheaper house** with Tom so one wage covers it.
feel: **Anxious**, but in the background like a dentist appointment.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough that I'd probably tell myself it's not real for the first three.
fieldNote: Chloe openly admits to **putting it off**, which fits her dislike of change.
Her trigger is seeing a **colleague** lose a job first.
Her father's **never stretch** rule shapes the smaller house decision.

steps.text: Start a weekend tyre-fitting course around year three
Buy a cheaper house with Tom so one wage covers the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, nobody knows what happens. I'd keep my head down. If people at the dairy talked about it, I'd change the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like a long time until you count it in school holidays, and then it's only ten summers of milk runs. I'd be 40 when the robots come. I'd probably have kids by then, so it scares me more in a quiet way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house with Tom and keep driving. Around 2032 I'd look properly at the garage or another job with my hands. I'd keep three months of bills in savings, always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared now, scared later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would kids change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, money-wise. I'd want to be home more, and a job at the garage nearer the house would fit that. Driving at six in the morning with a baby isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could make you feel calm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the dairy said, straight out, we'll keep people on and retrain them. Linda's fair, so maybe. But it's not Linda's decision, it's the owners'.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and nobody knows what happens.
I'd change the subject if colleagues **talked about it**.
think: Counted in **school holidays**, ten years is only ten summers of milk runs.
By **40** I'd likely have kids, which scares me more.
do: Buy the **house** with Tom and keep driving.
Always keep **three months** of bills saved.
feel: **Anxious**: not scared now, but scared later.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like a long time until you count it in school holidays, and then it's only ten summers of milk runs.
fieldNote: Chloe reframes a decade in **her own work rhythm**, and it shrinks.
Possible **children** make the late job loss feel heavier.
She'd only feel calm if the **owners** promised to retrain staff.

steps.text: Buy a small house with Tom while still driving
Look at garage jobs nearer home around 2032
Keep three months of bills saved at all times

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tom and I would both be hit and I'd have no gadget skills at all. What would help is the dairy telling us early and paying for training in something with hands, and some help with the mortgage if we'd bought by then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether I'd ever actually use these AI things. I wouldn't, not willingly. I'm not against progress, I'm against being the first one to try it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I'm against being the first one to try it.
portrait: Chloe Santos, 27, drives a **dairy fridge truck** to schools, cafés and village shops.
She likes routine and **paper notes**, and never uses AI tools.
In the fast picture she fears **both incomes** fall, since her boyfriend fixes exhausts at a garage.
With more time she admits she'd **delay** acting, but plans a cheaper house and garage work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her and her boyfriend hit and no tech skills to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Early warning and **paid hands-on training** from the dairy, plus mortgage help if needed.
